source_refs.note: Chapter 18 exercise (PDF 35-37), solved: 10 MCQs keyed with reasons (no key is printed), 15 short-answer, 3 constructed-response and 5 descriptive questions. MCQ VII, IX, Short l, m and the descriptive numbering carry Book corrections.

blocks.prompt: I. Which statement about the general physical properties of the first-row transition elements (titanium to copper) is incorrect?

options.text: They are typically soft solids at room temperature.
They are good conductors of heat and electricity.
They possess high melting and boiling points.

blocks.explanation: The first-row transition metals exist as hard and rigid solids, so “soft solids” is incorrect. High densities, high melting and boiling points and good conduction of heat and electricity are all correct.

blocks.prompt: II. The ability of transition elements to behave as catalysts is primarily linked to which of their properties:

options.text: Their ability to easily change oxidation states.

blocks.explanation: Transition metals and their compounds act as catalysts because they easily switch between stable oxidation states (e.g. Fe²⁺ ⇌ Fe³⁺), forming an intermediate that gives a pathway of lower activation energy and then regenerating the catalyst.

blocks.prompt: III. What is the reason for variable oxidation states in 3d transition metals?
blocks.explanation: The 3d and 4s subshells have very similar energies, so after the 4s electrons a variable number of 3d electrons can also be lost, giving several oxidation states.

blocks.prompt: IV. Which ionic configuration represents a metal that lost only its 4s electrons?
blocks.explanation:
Fe = [Ar] 3d⁶4s² → Fe²⁺ = [Ar] 3d⁶: only the two 4s electrons are lost.
Ti⁴⁺ (from 3d²4s²), V⁵⁺ (from 3d³4s²) and Sc³⁺ (from 3d¹4s²) have lost their 3d electrons as well.

blocks.prompt: V. In the complex ion, [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻, what is coordination number of central metal ion?
blocks.explanation: Fe²⁺ is bonded to six CN⁻ ligands by six dative bonds, so the coordination number is 6.

blocks.prompt: VI. The colour displayed by a transition metal complex is a result of electrons moving between d-orbitals. This process is called a:
blocks.explanation: An electron in a lower-energy d-orbital absorbs visible light and is promoted to a higher-energy d-orbital: a d-d transition. The colour seen is complementary to the light absorbed.

blocks.prompt: VII. Adding excess ammonia to pink [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ gives a yellow solution. What other changes occur besides colour change?

options.text: Oxidation state of Co changes form +2 to +3

blocks.explanation: [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 6NH₃ → [Co(NH₃)₆]²⁺ + 6H₂O. NH₃ replaces H₂O: the coordination number stays 6, cobalt stays +2 and the product is a solution. The new ligand changes the splitting ΔE, which changes the colour.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Option (b) prints “changes form +2 to +3”; the word is “from”.

blocks.prompt: VIII. Which one of the following complex has different geometry than others?
blocks.explanation: [CuCl₄]²⁻ has four ligands and is tetrahedral. The other three each have six ligands around Cu²⁺ and are octahedral.

blocks.prompt: IX. What geometry is typical when Co²⁺(aq) reacts with six monodentate anionic ligands?
blocks.explanation: The chapter states that aqueous cobalt(II) ions usually form tetrahedral complexes with monodentate anionic ligands such as Cl⁻, OH⁻ and SCN⁻, e.g. [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 4Cl⁻ → [CoCl₄]²⁻ (blue, tetrahedral). See the Book correction about “six”.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question says “six monodentate anionic ligands”, but a complex with six ligands bonded to the metal is octahedral. The tetrahedral complexes of Co²⁺ with anionic ligands, such as [CoCl₄]²⁻, have four ligands; the six-coordinate ion is the starting [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺. The key (d) follows the chapter's statement; read the question as “reacts with monodentate anionic ligands” (e.g. Cl⁻).

blocks.prompt: X. Optical isomers are characterized by their ability to rotate plane-polarized light. The isomer that rotates light to the right is called:
blocks.explanation: The isomer that rotates the plane of polarized light to the right (clockwise) is dextrorotatory (+); the one rotating it to the left is laevorotatory (–).

blocks.prompt: a) Why is zinc not included in the transition metals, although it shows electronic configuration with d-orbitals and also the member of d-block?
blocks.explanation: A transition element must have a partially filled d subshell in at least one stable oxidation state. Zinc forms only one ion, Zn²⁺ ([Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s⁰), whose 3d subshell is completely filled (Zn atom is also 3d¹⁰). So zinc is a d-block element but not a transition element.

blocks.prompt: b) What is the correlation between the ability of transition elements to exhibit variable oxidation states and their electron configuration.
blocks.explanation: The 3d and 4s subshells have comparable energies. A 3d metal first loses its 4s electrons (usually giving +2) and can then lose a variable number of 3d electrons, giving higher states. The more 3d + 4s electrons available, the higher the maximum state (Mn, 3d⁵4s², reaches +7); this gives the parabolic trend across the row.

blocks.prompt: c) How do transition metals function as effective catalysts. Give some examples.
blocks.explanation:
1. Variable oxidation states: the metal ion easily switches between states (Fe²⁺ ⇌ Fe³⁺), forms an unstable intermediate with the reactant and is regenerated, giving a lower-energy pathway (homogeneous catalysis), e.g. nickel salts (Ni(0)/Ni(II)) in making acrylic acid from acetylene.
2. Vacant, accessible d-orbitals: reactants are adsorbed on the metal surface in the correct orientation, lowering activation energy (heterogeneous catalysis), e.g. iron in the Haber process (N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃).

blocks.prompt: d) Why the complex [Cr(en)₃]³⁺ is more stable than [Cr(H₂O)₆]³⁺?
blocks.explanation: en (H₂NCH₂CH₂NH₂) is a bidentate ligand: each en bonds through two N atoms and forms a ring with Cr³⁺ (chelation), while H₂O is monodentate. Complexes of polydentate ligands have much higher stability constants (chelate effect), so [Cr(en)₃]³⁺ is more stable. (Beyond the chapter: 3 en replace 6 H₂O, so the number of free particles increases, which favours the chelate.)

blocks.prompt: e) Define a complex and the nature of the bond between its components.
blocks.explanation: A complex (coordination compound) is a molecule or ion in which a central metal atom or ion is surrounded by electron-pair donor species (ligands), e.g. [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻. Each ligand donates a lone pair into a vacant d-orbital of the metal, forming a coordinate covalent (dative) bond: the ligand acts as a Lewis base, the metal ion as a Lewis acid.

blocks.prompt: f) What is the coordination number? Give this number for [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻.
blocks.explanation: The coordination number is the total number of dative bonds formed between the ligands and the central metal atom or ion in a complex. In [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻, Fe²⁺ is bonded to six CN⁻ ligands, so the coordination number is 6.

blocks.prompt: g) Define a bidentate ligand and state how many bonds it forms to the central ion.
blocks.explanation: A bidentate ligand can donate two electron pairs (from two donor atoms) to the central metal atom or ion, so it forms two coordinate bonds. Examples: 1,2-diaminoethane (en, two N atoms) and ethanedioate ion C₂O₄²⁻ (two O atoms).

blocks.prompt: h) Draw the structure of EDTA ligand and label its electron pair donating sites.
blocks.explanation:
Structure (in words): EDTA⁴⁻ (ethylenediaminetetraacetate) is (⁻OOCCH₂)₂N–CH₂–CH₂–N(CH₂COO⁻)₂: two N atoms joined by a –CH₂–CH₂– bridge, each N carrying two –CH₂COO⁻ arms.
Donor sites (six): the lone pair on each of the 2 N atoms, and one O⁻ of each of the 4 carboxylate groups. So EDTA is a hexadentate ligand, e.g. Ca²⁺ + EDTA⁴⁻ → [Ca(EDTA)]²⁻.

blocks.prompt: i) Draw the colour wheel used to predict the colour of transition metal complexes. Also pair up the complementary colours with each other.
blocks.explanation:
Colour wheel (in words): a circle divided into six equal sectors in the order orange, yellow, green, blue, violet, red (going round the circle). Colours opposite each other are complementary:
Orange ↔ Blue
Yellow ↔ Violet
Green ↔ Red
A complex appears in the colour complementary to the light it absorbs, e.g. absorbs yellow → appears violet.

blocks.prompt: j) Define Kstab. How it reflects the stability of coordination complexes?
blocks.explanation:
Kstab is the equilibrium constant for the formation of a complex ion in solution from the hydrated metal ion and the new ligand, e.g.
[Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 4Cl⁻ ⇌ [CuCl₄]²⁻ + 6H₂O
Kstab = [[CuCl₄]²⁻] / ([[Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺][Cl⁻]⁴) (water omitted)
The higher Kstab (log₁₀ Kstab), the more stable the complex and the further the equilibrium lies to the right: [CuCl₄]²⁻ 5.6 < ammonia complex 13.1 < [Cu(EDTA)]²⁻ 18.8.

blocks.prompt: k) How coordination number 4 has two shapes i.e., tetrahedral and square planar?
blocks.explanation:
With four ligands the shape depends on the electronic configuration of the metal ion and the nature of the ligands:
Square planar (90°): typical of d⁸ ions (Ni²⁺, Pt²⁺) with ligands such as NH₃ and CN⁻, e.g. [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻, [Pt(NH₃)₄]²⁺.
Tetrahedral (109.5°): common for d⁷, d⁸ and d¹⁰ ions, often with Cl⁻, e.g. [CoCl₄]²⁻, [MnCl₄]²⁻.

blocks.prompt: l) Illustrate the type of isomerism shown by [PtNH₃)₂Cl₂] complex.
blocks.explanation:
[Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] is square planar and shows geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism:
cis (cisplatin): the two Cl (and the two NH₃) at adjacent corners, 90° apart; polar.
trans (transplatin): the two Cl at opposite corners, 180° apart; the bond dipoles cancel, non-polar.
The isomers have different properties: only cisplatin is an anticancer drug.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The formula is printed “[PtNH₃)₂Cl₂]” with a bracket missing; the complex is [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂].

blocks.prompt: m) Give medicinal importance of cis-plantin.
blocks.explanation: Cisplatin, cis-[Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂], is an anticancer drug. Inside the cell water replaces its chloride ligands; the activated drug binds to guanine bases of DNA and cross-links the double helix. This stops DNA replication in rapidly dividing cancer cells and triggers programmed cell death (apoptosis). Transplatin has no such action.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: “cis-plantin” is a misprint; the drug is cisplatin.

blocks.prompt: n) What happens when excess of ammonia solution is added to Co(II) hydroxide precipitates?
blocks.explanation:
The blue cobalt(II) hydroxide precipitate dissolves: NH₃ ligands replace the water and hydroxide ligands (ligand exchange), forming the soluble hexaamminecobalt(II) ion and a yellow solution:
[Co(H₂O)₄(OH)₂](s) + 6NH₃(aq) → [Co(NH₃)₆]²⁺(aq) + 4H₂O(l) + 2OH⁻(aq)

blocks.prompt: o) Is there any effect of excessive dilution of complexes? If yes then justify how does dilution affect the position of equilibrium in ligand ion exchange reactions?
blocks.explanation: Yes. Ligand exchange is an equilibrium, e.g. [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 4Cl⁻ ⇌ [CuCl₄]²⁻ + 6H₂O. Adding a large amount of water lowers the concentration of the new ligand (Cl⁻) and adds water ligand, so by Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium shifts to the left and the original hydrated ion re-forms (yellow-green back to blue).

blocks.prompt: a) Discuss the two types of stereoisomerism found in transition metal complexes. Use the examples [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] (square planar) and [Ni(NH₂CH₂CH₂NH₂)₃]²⁺ (octahedral) to illustrate the key structural differences that give rise to geometrical and optical isomerism, respectively.
blocks.explanation:
Stereoisomers have the same formula and bonds but a different arrangement of ligands in space.
1. Geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism, [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] (square planar): Pt and the four ligands lie in one plane at 90°. In the cis isomer the two Cl are adjacent (90°); in the trans isomer they are opposite (180°). The isomers cannot interconvert without breaking bonds and have different properties: cis is polar (cisplatin, anticancer), trans is non-polar (dipoles cancel).
2. Optical isomerism, [Ni(NH₂CH₂CH₂NH₂)₃]²⁺ (octahedral): three bidentate en ligands wrap around Ni²⁺ like a propeller, giving two forms that are non-superimposable mirror images (enantiomers). They have the same properties except that one rotates plane-polarized light to the right (dextrorotatory, +) and the other to the left (laevorotatory, –).
Key difference: geometrical isomers differ in the relative positions (90° or 180°) of the same ligands; optical isomers are mirror images, possible only when the complex has no plane of symmetry, as with three bidentate ligands.

rows: Same ligands at different relative positions (cis 90°, trans 180°)
Square planar and octahedral complexes, e.g. [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂]
Octahedral complexes with bidentate ligands, e.g. [Ni(en)₃]²⁺
Isomers differ in physical and chemical properties (dipole moment, drug action)
Same properties except the direction of rotation of plane-polarized light
One isomer is dextrorotatory (+), the other laevorotatory (–)

blocks.prompt:
b) The reaction between Cu²⁺ and I⁻ results in a solid precipitate of CuI and aqueous I₂.
a) Write down the two relevant reduction half-equations and their E° values (provided in the text).
b) Explain why comparing only the E° values suggests the reaction is not feasible as written.
c) Use Le Chatelier's principle to explain why the reaction proceeds forward in practice.
blocks.explanation:
a) Reduction half-equations (from the text):
½I₂(aq) + e⁻ → I⁻(aq)  E° = +0.54 V
Cu²⁺(aq) + e⁻ → Cu⁺(aq)  E° = +0.15 V
b) For 2Cu²⁺ + 4I⁻ → 2CuI + I₂, Cu²⁺ must be reduced and I⁻ oxidized:
E°cell = E°(reduction) − E°(oxidation) = 0.15 − 0.54 = −0.39 V
E°cell is negative; the I₂/I⁻ couple has the higher E°, so I₂ should be reduced instead, i.e. the reaction as written looks not feasible.
c) Cu⁺ formed is removed at once as the insoluble white precipitate CuI. Removing a product lowers [Cu⁺], so by Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium keeps shifting to the right, and the reaction goes forward (giving red-brown I₂).

blocks.prompt: c) Using the examples [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ and [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻, demonstrate how to predict the formula and overall charge of a complex ion. Clearly explain the role of the central metal ion charge, ligand charge, and coordination number in determining the final result for both examples.
blocks.explanation:
Rule: charge of complex = charge of metal ion + (coordination number × charge of one ligand). The coordination number gives the number of monodentate ligands written as a subscript; the formula is written metal first, then ligands, inside square brackets.
[Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺: metal Co³⁺ (+3); ligand NH₃ (ammine), neutral (0); coordination number 6 → Co(NH₃)₆.
Charge = (+3) + 6 × (0) = +3 → [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ (cationic complex)
[Fe(CN)₆]³⁻: metal Fe³⁺ (+3); ligand CN⁻ (cyano), −1; coordination number 6 → Fe(CN)₆.
Charge = (+3) + 6 × (−1) = −3 → [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻ (anionic complex)
So a neutral ligand leaves the metal's charge unchanged, while anionic ligands lower it and can make the complex negative. (With Fe²⁺ the same ligands give [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻.)

blocks.prompt: Q4. Explain the factors that determine the specific geometry (shape) of a transition metal complex.
blocks.explanation:
Transition metal complexes have definite shapes decided by:
1. Coordination number (number of donor atoms attached):
• 2 → linear, 180°: [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺, [Ag(CN)₂]⁻
• 4 → tetrahedral (109.5°) or square planar (90°)
• 6 → octahedral, four ligands in a square plane at 90° and two above and below at 180°: [Cr(NH₃)₆]³⁺, [Co(en)₃]³⁺ (the most common geometry)
2. Electronic configuration of the metal ion: d⁸ ions such as Ni²⁺ and Pt²⁺ give square planar complexes ([Ni(CN)₄]²⁻, [Pt(NH₃)₄]²⁺); tetrahedral complexes are common for d⁷, d⁸ and d¹⁰ ions ([CoCl₄]²⁻, [MnCl₄]²⁻).
3. Nature of the ligands: the same ion may change shape with the ligand. [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ and [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ are octahedral, but with Cl⁻ they give tetrahedral [CuCl₄]²⁻ and [CoCl₄]²⁻; Ni²⁺ with CN⁻ is square planar. (Beyond the chapter: large ligands such as Cl⁻ crowd each other, so fewer fit around the metal.)

blocks.prompt: Q3. Describe the splitting of d-orbitals and colour formation in octahedral and tetrahedral complexes.
blocks.explanation:
In a free metal ion the five d-orbitals (dxy, dxz, dyz, dx²−y², dz²) have the same energy (degenerate). When ligands approach, their electric field splits them into two sets of different energy; the gap is ΔE (Δ).
Octahedral (six ligands along the axes, e.g. [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺): dx²−y² and dz² point at the ligands and are raised (upper set of two); dxy, dxz, dyz are lower (set of three).
Tetrahedral (four ligands, e.g. [CuCl₄]²⁻): the pattern is inverted, dxy, dxz, dyz higher and dx²−y², dz² lower, and the splitting is smaller than in octahedral complexes.
Colour formation: an electron in the lower set absorbs visible light of energy ΔE = hν = hc/λ and is promoted to the upper set (d-d transition). The unabsorbed light is transmitted, and we see the complementary colour (absorbs yellow → appears violet; absorbs red/orange → appears blue or green).
The ligand affects ΔE: CN⁻ > en > NH₃ > H₂O > OH⁻ > Cl⁻ > Br⁻ > I⁻. A large ΔE means higher-frequency (violet/blue) light is absorbed and the complex looks yellow; a small ΔE means red/orange is absorbed and it looks blue or green. So changing the ligand or the geometry changes the colour.

rows: Six ligands along the x, y and z axes
Four ligands at the corners of a tetrahedron
Smaller splitting; the pattern is inverted

blocks.prompt: Q4. Compare the reactions of conc. HCl with aqueous Cu²⁺ and aqueous Co²⁺. Include equations, colour/geometry changes, and the reason for different colours.
blocks.explanation:
Cu²⁺(aq) is [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ (blue) and Co²⁺(aq) is [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ (pink). Conc. HCl added drop by drop supplies Cl⁻, which replaces the water ligands (ligand exchange):
[Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺(aq) + 4Cl⁻(aq) → [CuCl₄]²⁻(aq) + 6H₂O(l): blue → yellow (yellow-green) solution
[Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺(aq) + 4Cl⁻(aq) → [CoCl₄]²⁻(aq) + 6H₂O(l): pink → blue solution
In both, six water ligands are replaced by four Cl⁻: coordination number 6 → 4, geometry octahedral → tetrahedral, charge 2+ → 2−.
Reason for the colours: the new ligand and new shape change the d-orbital splitting ΔE. Cl⁻ causes a smaller splitting than H₂O, and tetrahedral splitting is smaller than octahedral, so light of a different frequency is absorbed and a different complementary colour is seen. Cu²⁺ (d⁹) and Co²⁺ (d⁷) have different d-electron numbers and splittings, so their chloro complexes show different colours (yellow and blue).

blocks.prompt: Q5. Describe the various redox reactions that takes place in transition metal complex ions?
blocks.explanation:
Transition metals exist in several oxidation states, so their ions take part in redox reactions. Feasibility is judged from standard electrode potentials: E°cell = E°(reduction) − E°(oxidation); the reaction is feasible if E°cell is positive. The half-reaction with the more positive E° is reduced.
1. Acidified manganate(VII) with ethanedioate:
MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O  E° = +1.52 V (×2)
C₂O₄²⁻ → 2CO₂ + 2e⁻ (×5)
2MnO₄⁻ + 16H⁺ + 5C₂O₄²⁻ → 2Mn²⁺ + 10CO₂ + 8H₂O
E°cell = 1.52 − (−0.49) = +2.01 V: feasible; MnO₄⁻ is the oxidizing agent, C₂O₄²⁻ the reducing agent.
2. Manganate(VII) with iron(II):
MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O  E° = +1.52 V
Fe³⁺ + e⁻ → Fe²⁺  E° = +0.77 V (reversed and ×5)
MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O
E°cell = 1.52 − 0.77 = +0.75 V: feasible.
3. Copper(II) with iodide:
2Cu²⁺(aq) + 4I⁻(aq) → 2CuI(s) (white) + I₂(aq) (red-brown)
Cu²⁺ + e⁻ → Cu⁺ E° = +0.15 V; ½I₂ + e⁻ → I⁻ E° = +0.54 V
E°cell = 0.15 − 0.54 = −0.39 V, yet the reaction goes forward because CuI precipitates and removes Cu⁺ (Le Chatelier's principle). The I₂ formed can be titrated with thiosulphate.
(The chapter prints E° = +0.49 V for 2CO₂/C₂O₄²⁻ and −0.77 V for Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ with E°cell +1.03 V and +2.29 V; its own correction notes give the standard values used here.)

blocks.prompt: Q6. Explain the stereoisomerism with its types in transition metal complexes.
blocks.explanation:
Stereoisomers are complexes with the same formula and bonds but a different arrangement of ligands in space. Two types:
1. Geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism: identical ligands are at adjacent positions (cis, 90°) or opposite positions (trans, 180°). Found in square planar and octahedral complexes.
• [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] (square planar): cis-isomer (cisplatin) has the two Cl adjacent and is polar; trans-isomer (transplatin) has them opposite, the dipoles cancel and it is non-polar. Cisplatin is an anticancer drug; transplatin is not.
• [Co(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]³⁺ (MA₄B₂ octahedral): cis (two H₂O at 90°) and trans (180°); only two geometrical isomers. Similarly [Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]⁺.
2. Optical isomerism: the isomers are non-superimposable mirror images (enantiomers). Common in octahedral complexes with bidentate ligands, e.g. [Ni(NH₂CH₂CH₂NH₂)₃]²⁺ ([Ni(en)₃]²⁺). The enantiomers have identical properties except that they rotate plane-polarized light in opposite directions: dextrorotatory (+) to the right, laevorotatory (–) to the left.

rows: Same ligands at different relative positions (cis 90°, trans 180°)
Square planar and octahedral complexes, e.g. [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂]
Octahedral complexes with bidentate ligands, e.g. [Ni(en)₃]²⁺
Isomers differ in physical and chemical properties (dipole moment, drug action)
Same properties except the direction of rotation of plane-polarized light
One isomer is dextrorotatory (+), the other laevorotatory (–)
